3. The defendant Nos. 1 to 3 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement denying the material allegations contained in the plaint and contended further that the defendant No. 1 never executed any bainanama with the plaintiff for the sale of the suit property, the defendant No. 1 never received any consideration money from the plaintiff as alleged; the said bainanama was fraudulently manufactured, it was nothing but a forged piece of paper. It was further stated by the defendants, that the defendant No. 1 transferred the suit property to defendant Nos. 2 and 3 by two registered deeds of sale dated 27.12.78 and 4.3.79 respectively and delivered possession thereof. Subsequently, the opposite party Nos. 2 and 3 have mutated their names in the Government record of rights and have been paying Government rent. Further case of defendant Nos. 2 and 3 is that they are bonafide purchasers for value without any notice of the alleged agreement for sale. 

 5. The learned trial Court on consideration of the evidence and other materials on record dismissed the suit holding that the suit was barred by limitation, the plaintiff failed to prove that the said agreement for sale was a genuine one or that it was executed by the defendant No. 1. The trial Court also found that no amount was paid to the defendant No. 1 as consideration for the agreement for sale. It was also held by the trial Court that the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 were bonafide purchasers for valuable consideration without notice of the so-called agreement for sale. 

 6. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree the plaintiff, as appellant preferred an appeal, being Appeal No. 392 of 1986 before the learned District Judge. The appeal was heard by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Mymensingh, who after hearing the parties and perusing the records, dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court, holding that the suit was barred by limitation, the plaintiff failed to prove any agreement for sale or its execution thereof by the defendant No. 1, nor the plaintiff could prove any payment of consideration money as alleged by him. Further the Appellate Court found that the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 were able to prove that they were the bonafide purchasers for value without notice of the so-called bainanama. Hence, this Rule has been issued at the instance of the plaintiff-petitioner. 

 18. Mr. Gour Gopal Saha, the learned Advocate for the opposite party Nos. 2 and 3, very forcefully submits that the Appellate Court, taking into account the facts and circumstances of the case and on consideration of evidence and other materials on record rightly rejected the prayer of the appellant for referring Exhibit 1 to the hand-writing expert for his opinion. Mr. Gour Gopal Saha has referred to the provisions of Order 41 rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure which reads as follows: 

 (2) Wherever additional evidence is allowed to be produced by an Appellate Court, the Court shall record the reason for its admission." 

 Let the LC Records be sent down expeditiously.
